opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things I find most exciting right now. When you train a model, you usually judge it by its outputs: the loss curve, benchmark scores, maybe some vibes from chatting with it. But that tells you very little about what's actually changing inside the network. Two checkpoints can look almost identical on evals and still have reorganized their internal representations quite a bit, or picked up some new behavior that hasn't surfaced in your test set yet.

With interpretability tools, we can start to do what I think of as a "diff" between checkpoints. Instead of just asking "did the score go up?", you can ask which features or concepts emerged, which ones got stronger or weaker, and which circuits got rewired. That's a much richer picture of what training actually did.

There are a few reasons that matters. The first is debugging. If a fine-tune introduces something you didn't want, like sycophancy, a weird refusal pattern, or a spurious correlation it latched onto from the data, you'd love to catch it at the level of mechanism rather than discovering it in production. Comparing checkpoints lets you localize when and where that shift happened.

The second is understanding learning dynamics. There's a lot we still don't know about how capabilities form. Do they come in gradually, or is there a phase transition where a circuit suddenly clicks into place? Watching features appear across checkpoints is like having a time-lapse of the model's development, and I think that's going to teach us a lot about training itself.

The third, and the one I'm most excited about longer term, is turning interpretability into something you use during training, not just after. If you can see what each step of training is doing to the model's internals, you can start to intervene. You can steer the process toward the representations you want and away from the ones you don't. That moves us from treating models as black boxes we poke at to actually designing them deliberately. Checkpoint comparison is one of the most natural on-ramps to that future.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What draws me to checkpoint comparison is that a training run is really a story, and most of the time we only read the last page. You get the final model, you benchmark it, you ship it. But the intermediate checkpoints tell you how it got there, and that "how" is where almost all the interesting science lives.

A few things in particular fascinate me. First, capabilities don't arrive smoothly. You'll see a skill like multi-step arithmetic or following a complex instruction sit flat for a long stretch and then jump, sometimes within a surprisingly narrow window of training. If you only look at the endpoint, you'd never know it happened that way, and you certainly couldn't ask why.

Second, comparing checkpoints is one of the few ways to separate what the model actually learned from what it happened to memorize or pick up early. If a behavior shows up at step ten thousand and never changes, that's a very different thing from one that's still shifting at the end of training. That distinction matters a lot for safety and for understanding generalization.

And third, it gives you a kind of controlled experiment for free. Same architecture, same data distribution, same everything except how far along it is. So when a representation inside the network changes between two checkpoints, you can be pretty confident the change is about training progress rather than some confound. That makes it a great setting for interpretability work, because you can watch a circuit form rather than reverse-engineer it after the fact.

So the short version is, the final model tells you what, and the checkpoints tell you how and when. I find the how and when much more interesting.
